title: How words change when you stop — tāʾ marbūṭah, maqṭūʿ and mawṣūl
objectives: Student can apply the nine changes a word undergoes at a stop, without prompting.
Student can tell a tāʾ marbūṭah ة from an open tāʾ ت in the printed word, and stop on each correctly — as a hāʾ and as a tāʾ respectively.
Student can say what rawm and ishmām are and when each is available.
Student can read maqṭūʿ and mawṣūl and say why the spelling constrains where she may stop.

slides.heading: Lesson 3.34 — How words change when you stop
Same word, two spellings, two stops
body: Stop on each of these, one after the other: سُنَّةَ ٱللَّهِ (48:23), then سُنَّتَ ٱلْأَوَّلِينَ (35:43).
Same word. Same meaning. You will stop on both the same way, almost certainly as sunnah.
Look at the two tāʾs. One is round with two dots — ة. One is open — ت. They are the same word, spelt two ways, in two different āyāt, and they stop differently: sunnah and sunnat.
The muṣḥaf is not being inconsistent. It is telling you something, and today you learn to hear what.
That is the whole lesson in one pair: the spelling is instruction. You have been taught for two units to read what is written; today you learn that the shape of the writing itself carries rules.

Ibn al-Jazarī gives these three topics one chapter, and they belong together for one reason: all three are about what the muṣḥaf's spelling tells you about where you may stop and what you say when you get there.

slides.heading: The nine changes
body: Stopping is not just silence. The last word physically changes shape. A learner who stops without applying these produces a word that does not exist in Arabic.
1. The final ḥarakah drops — the last letter becomes sākin. ٱلرَّحِيمِ → ٱلرَّحِيمْ.
2. Tāʾ marbūṭah becomes a sākin hāʾ. ة → هْ.
3. Tanwīn fatḥ becomes an alif, two counts — madd ʿiwaḍ. أَفْوَاجًا → afwājā.
4. Tanwīn ḍamm and tanwīn kasr simply drop. Plain sukūn, no madd. أَحَدٌ → aḥad.
5. Madd ʿāriḍ appears — a preceding madd letter takes your 2/4/6.
6. Madd līn appears — a preceding līn letter takes the same 2/4/6.
7. Qalqalah kubrā, if the final letter is a qalqalah letter.
8. Madd ṣilah drops — the connective madd on the pronoun hāʾ vanishes.
9. A final shaddah is retained, held, and leaned on.
Teach it as ONE table, not nine rules. And point out the arithmetic: you already do 1, 2, 5, 7 and — without knowing it — 3. Today adds 4, 6, 8 and 9. Four items, not nine.

slides.heading: Change 3 is not an addition
body: أَفْوَاجًا becomes afwājā at a stop. You are not adding an alif.
Look at the page: the alif is already printed there.
All that happened is that the tanwīn above it went quiet, leaving the alif to be read as what it is.
That framing costs ten seconds and saves you a rule. 2-12 gave it to you once already, and repeating it now is deliberate.

Four separate madd rules you already know — ʿiwaḍ, ʿāriḍ, līn, and the disappearance of ṣilah — are CONSEQUENCES of the one table. Framed that way, half of them stop being new material and become observations.

slides.translation: And you see the people entering into the religion of Allah in multitudes.

audio.cue: أَفْوَاجًا at a stop: the tanwīn fatḥ goes quiet and the alif already printed there is read at two counts. Madd ʿiwaḍ, change 3. Nothing was added.

slides.heading: The tāʾ marbūṭah, and the open-tāʾ exception
body: ة is read as a t when you join, and as a sākin هْ when you stop. The two dots exist for the joined reading. Stop, and you ignore them.
ٱلْمُوقَدَةُ (104:6) joined; ٱلْمُوقَدَهْ stopped. رِحْلَةَ ٱلشِّتَآءِ (106:2) joined; رِحْلَهْ if you stopped there. حَمَّالَةَ ٱلْحَطَبِ (111:4) — joined straight through, so the ة is a t.
Where the muṣḥaf writes an OPEN tāʾ, it stops as a plain sākin تْ, not as a hāʾ: رَحْمَتَ · نِعْمَتَ · سُنَّتَ · ٱمْرَأَتَ · كَلِمَتَ · شَجَرَتَ · لَعْنَتَ · فِطْرَتَ · ذَاتَ.
This is spelling, not grammar. There is no rule to derive; there is a shape on the page to obey.
And the same word can appear both ways — سُنَّةَ ٱللَّهِ (48:23) against سُنَّتَ ٱلْأَوَّلِينَ (35:43) — which is exactly why you must look rather than remember.
Say this out loud, because it is the transferable lesson: read what is written. The muṣḥaf's orthography is transmitted, not typeset. Where it looks irregular, the irregularity is the information.
You met one of these already: ذَاتَ in 111:3 is written with an open tāʾ, so it stops as dhāt. 2-12 gave it in passing; today it becomes a category.

slides.translation: Their accustomed security in the caravan of winter and summer.

audio.cue: رِحْلَةَ carries a tāʾ marbūṭah. Joined onward it is a t. Stop on it deliberately, for practice, and it becomes riḥlah — change 2. This is ikhtibārī stopping, from 3-33, and naming it is part of the drill.

slides.heading: Rawm and ishmām
body: Two optional refinements at a stop. They are available, not required.
Rawm — الروم. Pronounce about one third of the final vowel: audible, very soft. Available on ḍammah and kasrah only, never on fatḥah.
Ishmām — الإشمام. Round the lips immediately after the sukūn, silently: visible, inaudible. Available on ḍammah only.
Demonstrate rawm on ٱلرَّحِيمِ, which ends in a kasrah, and ishmām on نَسْتَعِينُ, which ends in a ḍammah. Have her watch your mouth for the ishmām — the whole point is that it is seen and not heard.
Neither is required of her at the Final Checkpoint, and she should be told that.

They are here because she will see reciters do them, and because ishmām is the mechanism behind the one Ḥafṣ-specific word she must eventually know: لَا تَأْمَ۫نَّا at Yūsuf 12:11, the only ishmām in Ḥafṣ.

slides.heading: Al-maqṭūʿ wa'l-mawṣūl — separated and joined
body: Some word pairs are written APART — maqṭūʿ — and some are written JOINED — mawṣūl. The Uthmānī spelling is not free variation; it is fixed and transmitted.
Written apart, from outside your memorised surahs: مِّن مَّا مَلَكَتْ (30:28) · فِى مَآ ءَاتَىٰكُم (5:48) · أَن لَّآ أَقُولَ (7:105) · مَالِ هَٰذَا ٱلْكِتَٰبِ (18:49).
Written joined: وَمِمَّا رَزَقْنَٰهُمْ (2:3) · فِيمَا كَانُوا۟ (2:113) · أَلَّا تَعْبُدُوٓا۟ (11:2).
The rule you need, in one line: written apart → the two are separate words, so a stop between them is possible. Written joined → it is one word, and you never stop inside a word.
That connects straight back to 2-12: never stop in the middle of a word. Whether something IS one word is decided by the page, not by grammar.
مَالِ هَٰذَا ٱلْكِتَٰبِ (18:49) is the memorable one: مَا and لِ, written with a gap. It looks like a typographic accident and it is not.
Keep this short and concrete. You need the principle plus four examples, not the classical list of every case.

audio.cue: أَحَدٌ at a stop runs two changes: the tanwīn ḍamm simply drops — change 4, plain sukūn, no madd — and the dāl bounces, change 7. Two changes, no length anywhere.

slides.translation: May the hands of Abū Lahab be ruined, and ruined is he.

audio.cue: وَتَبَّ at the stop: change 9. A final shaddah is held, with emphasis. Stopping feels like ending and ending feels like relaxing — lean on the bāʾ instead. Two of them, and then stop.

slides.translation: Who has fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear.

audio.cue: The last word of Sūrat Quraysh, which you completed last session, runs three of the nine changes at once: the tanwīn kasr drops (4), the līn wāw appears at your chosen 2/4/6 (6), and the fāʾ closes on a clean sukūn (1). Produce it slowly, naming each change as it happens, then at speed.

pairs.note: Changes 1 and 5. The final kasrah drops, the nūn goes sākin, and the yāʾ before it becomes a madd ʿāriḍ at your chosen 2/4/6.
Change 3. Tanwīn fatḥ goes quiet and the alif already printed is read at two counts. Madd ʿiwaḍ — an addition of nothing.
Changes 4 and 7. Tanwīn ḍamm simply drops — no alif, no madd — and the dāl takes qalqalah kubrā.
Changes 1, 4 and 6, all at once. Tanwīn kasr drops, the līn wāw appears at your number, and the fāʾ closes on a clean sukūn.

slides.heading: Join it, stop it, name the change
slides.instructions: For each word: read it joined, then stopped, then tell me which numbered change you applied. Slowly at first — accuracy before pace.

audio.cue: 1 and 5. The kasrah drops and the yāʾ becomes a madd ʿāriḍ at your number.
3. Tanwīn fatḥ goes quiet; the printed alif is read at two.
4 and 7. Tanwīn ḍamm drops, dāl bounces, nothing lengthens.
1 and 5. And this is the one to demonstrate ishmām on — watch my mouth, do not listen for it.
1, 4 and 6. Three at once, and it is the last word of a surah you recite daily.
9. Hold the bāʾ. Two of them, and then stop. Lean on it.
2. Tāʾ marbūṭah becomes a sākin hāʾ: riḥlah. Cover the two dots with your fingernail — what letter is it now?
104:6 — 2 again. al-mūqadah, not al-mūqadat.

slides.heading: The two tāʾs — round or open
slides.instructions: Before reading, say ROUND or OPEN. Then stop on each: hāʾ for round, tāʾ for open. Look, do not remember. The same word appears both ways in the Qurʾān, which is exactly why looking is the only method that works.

audio.cue: 48:23 — ROUND. Stops as sunnah.
35:43 — OPEN. Stops as sunnat. Same word, different spelling, different stop.
7:56 — OPEN. Stops as raḥmat, not raḥmah. This is where the over-correction lands fifteen minutes after change 2 is taught.
106:2 — ROUND. Stops as riḥlah.
111:4 — ROUND, but you join straight through, so it is a t here. The change only fires if you actually stop.
111:3 — OPEN. Stops as dhāt. You met this one in passing at 2-12; today it belongs to a category.

slides.heading: Apart, or joined
slides.instructions: Say whether each is written apart or joined, and whether a stop is possible inside it. Then open the muṣḥaf to 18:49 and find مَالِ.

audio.cue: 30:28 — APART. Maqṭūʿ. Two words, so a stop between them is possible.
2:3 — JOINED. Mawṣūl. One word, so you never stop inside it. The same two words as the item before, spelt differently.
7:105 — APART.
11:2 — JOINED. Is there a space? No. Then it is one word.
18:49 — APART, and the memorable one. مَا and لِ written with a gap. It looks like a typographic accident and it is not.

mistakes.wrong: ة read as a t at a stop — al-mūqadat, raḥmah written round but stopped as a t.
mistakes.why: The two dots are right there, and Unit 2 spent a whole lesson teaching her to read the dots. She may also have heard the -at form in loanwords in her own language.
mistakes.fix: Cover the two dots with your fingernail. What letter is it now? Say that.

mistakes.wrong: Stopping on an OPEN tāʾ as a hāʾ — raḥmah for رَحْمَتَ.
mistakes.why: Brand-new over-correction from change 2, taught fifteen minutes earlier.
mistakes.fix: Look at the shape. Is it round or open? Open stays a t.

mistakes.wrong: The final ḥarakah still audible — nastaʿīnu, aḥadun.
mistakes.why: The vowel is printed and she is obeying the page. Give her credit for this when you correct it; it is obedience, not carelessness.
mistakes.fix: The page is written for joining. When you stop, the last mark is not yours.

mistakes.wrong: The ṣilah madd kept at a stop — lahū instead of lah.
mistakes.why: The little wāw is printed after the hāʾ and looks like a letter.
mistakes.fix: That mark only exists to carry you to the next word. You're not going there.

mistakes.wrong: A final shaddah released single — wa-tab for وَتَبَّ.
mistakes.why: Stopping feels like ending and ending feels like relaxing.
mistakes.fix: Hold the bāʾ. Two of them, and then stop. Lean on it.

mistakes.wrong: Stopping inside a mawṣūl word — a breath between the two halves of مِمَّا.
mistakes.why: She knows the grammar says two words and she is trusting the grammar over the page.
mistakes.fix: Is there a space? No. Then it is one word, and you never stop inside a word.

mistakes.wrong: Attempting rawm or ishmām and producing a full vowel.
mistakes.why: A third of a vowel is genuinely hard, and she is overshooting.
mistakes.fix: That was the whole vowel. Try a third of it — or leave it out entirely. Neither is required of you.

slides.heading: One stop, every change it fires

audio.cue: 1 and 5 — ḥarakah drops, madd ʿāriḍ appears at your number.
3 — tanwīn fatḥ becomes the alif that was already printed. Two counts.
4 and 7 — tanwīn ḍamm drops with no madd, and the dāl bounces.
9 — the shaddah is held and leaned on, not released single.
1, 4 and 6 together — the whole table running on one word from your own hifz.

slides.heading: Homework
tasks: Hifz: al-Fīl 105:1–2 to 20–40 repetitions daily — the last surah of the set begins today. Sabqi is al-Kawthar, al-Māʿūn and Quraysh, all whole. Manzil rotation first, ten extra repetitions after any caught error. Drill أَلَمْ تَرَ against أَلَمْ يَجْعَل as a pair: nearly identical openings are the classic place for a transposition error, and transposition is scored on the memorisation-fidelity axis separately from tajweed.

Find eight words in the muṣḥaf written with an OPEN tāʾ. Write each with its reference and read each one stopped. They are rarer than the round ones, and hunting for them is how you learn to see them.
Copy the nine-change table by hand onto a card. Nine rows. By hand.
One page a day: stop at āyah ends and apply EVERY change that word calls for. Mark on the page any stop you were unsure about, and bring the page.

Recite Sūrat Quraysh and stop deliberately on مِّنْ خَوْفٍۭ with the līn at your chosen count. Then recite al-Masad and stop on وَتَبَّ with the shaddah held. Two stops, two different rules, both from surahs you already hold.

audio.cue: ROUND — sunnah.
OPEN — sunnat.
OPEN — raḥmat.
ROUND — riḥlah.

drills.title: Apart or joined
drills.instructions: Say apart or joined, and whether a stop is possible inside. The page decides, not the grammar.

audio.cue: APART — a stop between them is possible.
JOINED — one word, never stop inside it.
APART.

dailyChecklist: Al-Fīl 105:1–2 to 20–40 repetitions, with أَلَمْ تَرَ and أَلَمْ يَجْعَل drilled as a pair
One page with stops at āyah ends and every change applied, unsure stops marked in pencil
Round-or-open called on six words before reading any of them
Quraysh stopped deliberately on مِّنْ خَوْفٍۭ, and al-Masad stopped on وَتَبَّ with the shaddah held

script: Open on the سُنَّةَ / سُنَّتَ pair and let her stop on both the same way. Then show her the two shapes. The whole lesson is in that pair: the spelling is instruction, and where the orthography looks irregular the irregularity is the information.

Teach the nine changes as one table, not as nine rules. Then do the arithmetic out loud: she already does five of them, so today adds four items. That reframing is worth a great deal on a slide that otherwise looks like a wall.
Repeat the 'change 3 is not an addition' framing from 2-12 deliberately. Ten seconds spent showing her the alif already printed on the page saves her a rule she would otherwise memorise.
Point out that ʿiwaḍ, ʿāriḍ, līn and the disappearance of ṣilah are consequences of this table rather than four separate madd rules. Half of today's material stops being new the moment she sees that.

On the open tāʾ, insist she LOOKS. There is nothing to derive here, and the same word appears both ways in the muṣḥaf, so any strategy based on remembering the word rather than reading the shape will fail.
Expect the over-correction on the open tāʾ within fifteen minutes of teaching change 2, and be ready for it rather than surprised by it.

Teach rawm and ishmām as available, not required, and say plainly that neither is asked of her at the Final Checkpoint. Demonstrate ishmām with her watching your mouth — it is seen and not heard, and that is the entire point.
Keep maqṭūʿ and mawṣūl short and concrete: the principle plus four examples. The classical list of every case is not what she needs and it will crowd out the tāʾ material, which is.

Finish on مِّنْ خَوْفٍۭ with three changes running at once. Have her produce it slowly, naming each change as it happens, then at speed. It is the last word of a surah she completed last session, so it is not a hypothetical.

When you ask her to stop on a word to show its waqf form, name it as ikhtibārī. She learned the category last lesson and hearing it applied to what you are both doing right now is what makes it stick.

listenFor.item: A stopped word that is a word — if what she produced is not a possible Arabic form, one of the nine did not fire.
listenFor.commonMistake: The final ḥarakah still audible: nastaʿīnu, aḥadun.
listenFor.whyItHappens: The vowel is printed and she is obeying the page. Give her credit for this when you correct it — it is obedience, not carelessness.
listenFor.correctionCue: The page is written for joining. When you stop, the last mark is not yours.

listenFor.item: Tāʾ marbūṭah stopped as a hāʾ, and an open tāʾ stopped as a tāʾ.
listenFor.commonMistake: ة read as a t at a stop, or — fifteen minutes later — an open tāʾ read as a hāʾ.
listenFor.whyItHappens: The two dots are right there and Unit 2 taught her to read the dots. The reverse error is over-correction from change 2, taught minutes earlier, and both appear in the same session.
listenFor.correctionCue: Cover the two dots with your fingernail. What letter is it now? And for the other one: look at the shape — open stays a t.

listenFor.item: The ṣilah madd disappearing at a stop — lah, not lahū.
listenFor.commonMistake: Keeping the connective madd on the pronoun hāʾ.
listenFor.whyItHappens: The little wāw is printed after the hāʾ and looks like a letter rather than like a connector.
listenFor.correctionCue: That mark only exists to carry you to the next word. You're not going there.

listenFor.item: A final shaddah still doubled and leaned on at the stop.
listenFor.whyItHappens: Stopping feels like ending and ending feels like relaxing, so the last letter is the first thing to lose effort.
listenFor.correctionCue: Hold the bāʾ. Two of them, and then stop. Lean on it.

listenFor.item: No breath taken inside a word written joined.
listenFor.commonMistake: A stop between the two halves of مِمَّا.
listenFor.whyItHappens: She knows the grammar says two words and she is trusting the grammar over the page.
listenFor.correctionCue: Is there a space? No. Then it is one word, and you never stop inside a word.

listenFor.item: Rawm at about a third of the vowel, or omitted entirely — never a full vowel wearing the name.
listenFor.commonMistake: Attempting rawm or ishmām and producing the whole vowel.
listenFor.whyItHappens: A third of a vowel is genuinely difficult and she is overshooting. Neither refinement is required of her, so overshooting has no upside.
listenFor.correctionCue: That was the whole vowel. Try a third of it — or leave it out entirely. Neither is required of you.

teacherNotes.homework: Daily: al-Fīl 105:1–2 to 20–40 repetitions with al-Kawthar, al-Māʿūn and Quraysh as Sabqi and the Manzil rotation first, ten extra after any caught error, and أَلَمْ تَرَ drilled back to back against أَلَمْ يَجْعَل because near-identical openings are the classic transposition trap; one page a day read stopping at āyah ends with every change applied and any uncertain stop pencilled and brought in. Written: the nine-change table copied by hand onto a card, nine rows; eight words found with an OPEN tāʾ, each with its reference, each read stopped. Once in the week: Quraysh recited with a deliberate stop on مِّنْ خَوْفٍۭ at her chosen līn count, and al-Masad with a deliberate stop on وَتَبَّ with the shaddah held.
